ocar.opportunity: Accurate 3D nuclei segmentation anchors cellular identity to circuit reconstruction, but even extensively proofread FAFB and MICrONS nuclei still contain last-mile errors.
ocar.challenge: Those errors are rare and heterogeneous—false merges from weak boundaries, false splits from z-axis artifacts, missing slices—and local pairwise fragment matching cannot resolve the global topology of densely packed nuclear clusters.
ocar.action: Wang, Liu, Zhao, Wang, Wan, Nie, and Wei present NuGraph on bioRxiv (2026): erroneous masks are decomposed into atomic 3D primitives, encoded with a point-cloud backbone, grouped by graph attention plus a primitive–proposal contrastive loss, then morphologically restored with a signed-distance-field refinement network. Training uses a self-supervised engine that synthesizes errors from clean nuclei labels.
ocar.resolution: On NucEMFix, a brain-wide EM benchmark of 8,000+ annotated error nuclei, NuGraph attains 87.99% F1 on NucEMFix-F (FAFB) and 86.20% on NucEMFix-M (MICrONS), outperforming re-segmentation baselines (for example +8.6% over nnU-Net) and pairwise correction methods. The authors report more than a 100× reduction in curation effort relative to manual proofreading.
ocar.future_work: The data engine uses clean masks alone, so severe imaging artifacts and missing slices that destroy structural continuity remain hard cases, especially in NucEMFix-M. Future work will couple error generation to raw EM imagery and explore image-conditioned graph reasoning.

summaries.beginner: Nucleus outlines in huge electron-microscope brain maps still get stuck together or split apart. This team treats the broken pieces as a graph, groups them back into whole nuclei, and reports that the cleanup is far faster than doing it by hand.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2026) and formatted as an IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging preprint, Wang and colleagues introduce NuGraph for last-mile 3D nuclei correction in connectomics. Primitives from decomposed error masks are reasoned over globally rather than as isolated pairs, then refined with an SDF head; training needs no manual error labels. On NucEMFix across FAFB and MICrONS they report 87.99% and 86.20% F1, beating nnU-Net and pairwise methods, with staged runtimes on the order of tens of minutes versus >100 hours of manual work for some error types. Failure cases in the extract include deep invaginations, large contact surfaces, and misalignment plus illumination artifacts.
summaries.advanced: NucEMFix is an error-case benchmark, not a claim that FAFB or MICrONS nuclei are now fully corrected. The +8.6% figure is versus nnU-Net specifically. The 100× curation claim is relative to manual proofreading as stated by the authors; the extract’s timing table is for their staged pipeline, not an independent time-motion study. Geometry-only synthetic errors cannot represent missing-slice failures that leave the reasoner without usable structure.

plain_language_summary: Nucleus outlines in huge electron-microscope brain maps still get stuck together or split apart. This team treats the broken pieces as a graph, groups them back into whole nuclei, and reports that the cleanup is far faster than doing it by hand.

ocar.opportunity: Taste drives feeding, foraging, and social behavior, yet gustation has remained among the least mapped sensory modalities at electron-microscopy connectome scale.
ocar.challenge: Gustatory receptor neurons are distributed across body parts, sexually dimorphic, and continuously modulated by internal state, and a wiring-level map spanning brain, cervical connective, and ventral nerve cord in both sexes was lacking.
ocar.action: Tastekin, de Haan Vicente, Beresford, Morris, Beckett, Schlegel, Costa, Jefferis, and Ribeiro post on bioRxiv (2025) a reconstruction of adult male Drosophila GRNs from all peripheral organs in a contiguous EM volume, then integrate it with existing female and male datasets into a pan-CNS, cross-sex connectome.
ocar.resolution: Connectivity-based clustering, molecular identity assignment, and dimorphism analysis type GRNs; all feeding motor neurons are mapped; and sensory-to-motor and neuroendocrine pathways are traced, revealing distinct architectures for nutrient assessment, motor control, neuroendocrine regulation, and courtship.
ocar.future_work: The conclusion treats cell typing and effective-connectivity analysis as a source of testable hypotheses for neurogenetic follow-up on descending bottlenecks, neuroendocrine coupling, and sexual dimorphisms, using existing Drosophila genetic tools.

summaries.beginner: Taste cells in the fruit fly sit on several body parts and steer feeding and courtship, but their full wiring was missing. This team reconstructs those sensors through brain and nerve cord and sketches how taste reaches muscles, hormones, and social circuits.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2025), Tastekin and colleagues report what they call the first complete wiring diagram of the adult Drosophila gustatory system, reconstructing GRNs in a contiguous male EM volume spanning brain, cervical connective, and VNC. Integration with existing datasets yields a pan-CNS, cross-sex connectome used for connectivity clustering, molecular identity mapping, and sexual-dimorphism analysis. They also map feeding motor neurons and trace GRN pathways to motor and endocrine targets, predicting transformations into feeding, foraging, ingestion, social behavior, and feedforward neuroendocrine regulation. Methods in the extract include Split-Gal4 immunostaining of female brains and VNC as a companion to the EM work.
summaries.advanced: “Complete” and “first” are authorship claims for the male peripheral-to-CNS reconstruction plus integration, not an independent census of every GRN in every existing volume. Predicted sensorimotor transformations are computational, not fully causal in this extract. Acknowledgments note pre-publication access to the male CNS dataset from FlyEM. Catalog tags emphasize FANC/MANC; the extract itself stresses a contiguous brain–connective–VNC male volume plus existing female and male maps.

plain_language_summary: Taste cells in the fruit fly sit on several body parts and steer feeding and courtship, but their full wiring was missing. This team reconstructs those sensors through brain and nerve cord and sketches how taste reaches muscles, hormones, and social circuits.

ocar.opportunity: Synaptic connectomes now list connections among up to on the order of 10^5 neurons, and many circuit models encode latent variables as approximate symmetries in wiring.
ocar.challenge: Those symmetries are noisy, and standard graph embeddings mix cell-type structure with the rotational or translational structure one actually wants to find. Exact graph automorphism algorithms also assume perfect equivalence of nodes.
ocar.action: Shan and Litwin-Kumar present on bioRxiv (2025) a graph-embedding algorithm that segregates cell-type structure from the symmetries of interest, motivated by ring attractors, convolutional visual weights, and grid-cell models.
ocar.resolution: The method identifies rotational and translational symmetries in heading-direction and visual projection neuron circuits of an adult Drosophila brain connectome, and a toroidal symmetry in a synthetic medial-entorhinal grid-cell connectome.
ocar.future_work: The extract develops a numerical test for “phase shift structure” between cell types via relative rotations of embeddings; a supplement embeds the entire hemibrain at once, but the selected text does not fully evaluate whole-brain discovery performance.

summaries.beginner: Some brain circuits are wired as if neurons sit on a ring or a map of space. This paper learns a layout of the fly’s wiring that reveals those hidden shapes, helping guess what variables a circuit is computing.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2025), Shan and Litwin-Kumar introduce a graph embedding designed to separate cell-type heterogeneity from approximate connectivity symmetries linked to computation. Unlike standard embeddings cited in the introduction, the method is built to recover rotational and translational structure. Applied to an adult Drosophila brain connectome it recovers symmetries in heading-direction and visual projection neuron circuits, and on a synthetic grid-cell connectome it recovers a torus. Embedding geometries are presented as revealing both latent variables and the cell types that implement them.
summaries.advanced: The Drosophila application is to heading and visual projection circuits, not a claim that all hemibrain cell types are symmetrically embedded. The grid-cell result is on a synthetic connectome. Approximate symmetry is the target; the authors note that exact automorphism is a different, classical problem. Phase-shift detection and whole-hemibrain sorting appear in the later extract but without full quantitative discovery metrics in the selected text.

plain_language_summary: Some brain circuits are wired as if neurons sit on a ring or a map of space. This paper learns a layout of the fly’s wiring that reveals those hidden shapes, helping guess what variables a circuit is computing.

ocar.opportunity: If gene expression could be steered before synapses form, small organisms or organoids might develop into task-specific biological agents as a path toward synthetic biological intelligence.
ocar.challenge: Existing connectome models do not mechanistically tie genetic expression and protein-interaction probabilities to synaptic multiplicity in a form that can be optimized end-to-end with task performance.
ocar.action: Boccato, Ferrante, and Toschi introduce SynaptoGen (arXiv:2402.07242, versions through 2025), a differentiable Connectome Models member in which synaptic weights equal average synapse counts times conductance derived from genetic profiles.
ocar.resolution: In simulated synaptogenesis, agents solved four reinforcement-learning benchmarks and consistently surpassed control baselines.
ocar.future_work: The authors flag remaining gaps in biological realism—the event-driven nature of biological networks, the synapse model, and feedforward topologies—and propose adaptations for spiking networks, positional embeddings for distance-dependent connectivity, and experimental data to refine circuit-level properties.

summaries.beginner: The idea is to set a neuron’s genes so that the synapses it grows already implement a useful circuit. This paper offers a math model of that process and tests it only in simulations of learning tasks.
summaries.intermediate: On arXiv (2402.07242; this extract is v3, 7 September 2025), Boccato, Ferrante, and Toschi present SynaptoGen as a differentiable map from gene expression and protein-interaction probabilities to synaptic multiplicity. Because the map is differentiable, genetic quantities and downstream task performance can be optimized jointly. Validation is in simulated synaptogenesis on four reinforcement-learning benchmarks, where derived agents outperformed the paper’s control baselines. The authors describe it as a member of the Connectome Models family aimed at pre-wired biological agents.
summaries.advanced: There is no wet-lab synaptogenesis or organoid result in the extract. “First model of its kind” is an authorship claim. Biological-realism gaps are acknowledged in the conclusions (spiking, synapse model, feedforward wiring). Catalog metadata lack a journal and DOI; the PDF is the arXiv preprint. Do not read the four-benchmark success as evidence that living circuits can yet be genetically programmed this way.

plain_language_summary: The idea is to set a neuron’s genes so that the synapses it grows already implement a useful circuit. This paper offers a math model of that process and tests it only in simulations of learning tasks.

ocar.opportunity: Large-scale extracellular spike recordings are widely used to infer circuit architecture, but how faithfully they recover synapses remains disputed.
ocar.challenge: Inference quality depends on the dynamical regime of spontaneous activity, connection type, and the amount of spike-train data, and many algorithms struggle to detect inhibitory connections.
ocar.action: Donner, Bartram, Hornauer, Kim, Roqueiro, Hierlemann, Obozinski, and Schröter post on bioRxiv (2024) a comparison framework using simulated networks plus empirical ground truth from parallel single-cell patch-clamp and HD-MEA recordings in vitro, then train an ensemble artificial neural network (eANN) on the validated outputs of six established inference algorithms.
ocar.resolution: The eANN was more robust across dynamical regimes and shorter recordings, improved identification of synaptic connections especially inhibitory ones, and better captured network topology. A SHAP analysis is used to interpret which input-method features drive the ensemble.
ocar.future_work: Ground truth in the extract is simulated or in-vitro HD-MEA/patch-clamp, not in-vivo EM-verified synapses. The selected text is truncated into supplements (method-weight correlations; training-simulation table), so generalization beyond those regimes is not demonstrated here.

summaries.beginner: Watching spikes is easier than seeing synapses, but turning spike trains into a wiring diagram is error-prone. This team tests several inference recipes against known connections in dishes and simulations, then combines them with a neural net that does better, especially on inhibitory links.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (1 February 2024), Donner and colleagues benchmark connectivity-from-spikes algorithms on synthetic data and on parallel patch-clamp plus HD-MEA recordings. They report large algorithm-to-algorithm differences and systematic trouble with inhibition, then introduce an ensemble ANN trained on six established methods’ outputs. The eANN improved accuracy and robustness across dynamical regimes and shorter recordings and, they argue, improved topological characterization of the networks. Author-summary SHAP analysis is offered as an interpretation of feature importance.
summaries.advanced: This is functional-connectivity inference, not EM connectomics. Empirical ground truth is three single-cell patch recordings in parallel with HD-MEA in vitro. “Synaptic connections” in the title should be read as inferred, validated against that ground truth. The extract does not name the six base algorithms in the retained abstract/summary block (a supplement mentions GLMCC and GLMPP among correlated methods).

plain_language_summary: Watching spikes is easier than seeing synapses, but turning spike trains into a wiring diagram is error-prone. This team tests several inference recipes against known connections in dishes and simulations, then combines them with a neural net that does better, especially on inhibitory links.

ocar.opportunity: Synapse-resolution connectomes invite tools that predict function from wiring; C. elegans, with a mapped nervous system of 302 neurons, is a natural prototype.
ocar.challenge: Whether fiber (fibration) symmetries in the locomotive subnetworks predict cluster synchronization, and how they compare with stricter orbit symmetries, was unclear, especially once chemical synapses and gap junctions are treated separately.
ocar.action: Avila, Serafino, Augusto, Zimmer, and Makse in PLoS ONE (2024) search graph symmetries in symmetrized forward and backward locomotive subnetworks, validate predictions with admissible ODE simulations, and decompose the graphs into nested-loop or multilayer fiber building blocks.
ocar.resolution: Fiber symmetries predicted neuronal synchronization even under non-idealized connectivity when dynamics stayed in stable regimes. Minimal balanced coloring captured synchronicity patterns, performing best with synaptic interactions present; orbit colorings were weaker for the ODE models used. Undirected gap-junction networks globally synchronized under constant input and recovered predicted groups mainly under sinusoidal or random drive.
ocar.future_work: The study used a repaired connectome, identical biophysical node/edge properties, and isolated chemical versus gap-junction networks. The authors plan experimental recordings and circuit interrogation, and suggest applying the approach to larval or adult fly connectomes.

summaries.beginner: If two neurons are wired as copies of each other, they may fire in lockstep. This paper looks for those copy-paste patterns in the worm’s walking circuits and checks the idea in simulations.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS ONE (2024), Avila and colleagues analyze fibration symmetries in symmetrized forward and backward locomotive subnetworks of C. elegans. ODE simulations admissible to the graphs are used to test fiber versus more restrictive orbit symmetries, and fibrations decompose the graphs into nested-loop or multilayer building blocks. Fiber symmetries predicted synchronization within stable dynamical regimes; balanced coloring outperformed orbit coloring for the synaptic ODE setting, consistent with neurons depending on inputs rather than out-degree. Isolated gap-junction networks behaved differently under constant versus time-varying drive.
summaries.advanced: Connectivity is symmetrized and, in places, repaired; biophysics are idealized and identical across nodes. Chemical and gap-junction graphs are analyzed in isolation, not as a single mixed network. Synchronization is simulated, not measured in the worm. The 302-neuron census is the classical mapped nervous system cited in the introduction. Predictions about locomotor ensembles remain to be tested experimentally, as the authors state.

plain_language_summary: If two neurons are wired as copies of each other, they may fire in lockstep. This paper looks for those copy-paste patterns in the worm’s walking circuits and checks the idea in simulations.

ocar.opportunity: A comprehensive synaptic map of an animal circadian clock would show how diverse daily physiology and behavior are orchestrated.
ocar.challenge: The Drosophila circadian network was classically counted at about 150 neurons, with incomplete knowledge of contralateral coupling, light-input routes, and how sparsely clock cells contact higher-order and neurosecretory targets.
ocar.action: Reinhard, Fukuda, Manoli, Derksen, Saito, Möller, Sekiguchi, Rieger, Helfrich-Förster, Yoshii, and Zandawala in Nature Communications (2024) build a connectivity map from the FlyWire female brain connectome and integrate single-cell transcriptomics with receptor mapping to infer putative paracrine peptidergic signaling.
ocar.resolution: They identify additional dorsal clock neurons, raising the network to about 240 rather than 150 cells, report extensive contralateral synapses, describe novel indirect light-input pathways, and map routes onto descending neurons that regulate feeding and reproduction. Monosynaptic contacts to many downstream centers are sparse, so they argue peptidergic signaling enriches interconnectivity and identify additional neuropeptides in clock neurons.
ocar.future_work: Synaptic and paracrine links are explicitly predictions pending functional tests. The authors did not map gap junctions, photoreceptor-axon proofreading was incomplete in the FlyWire version used, and they generally required more than 4 synapses. Both FlyWire and hemibrain are adult female brains.

summaries.beginner: The fly’s daily clock was thought to be about 150 neurons. Using a whole-brain wiring map, this team finds more clock cells, left–right connections, extra light routes, and a likely big role for peptide signals rather than only direct synapses.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2024), Reinhard and colleagues generate a comprehensive Drosophila clock connectivity map from FlyWire. They report ~240 clock neurons (additional dorsal cells versus the classical ~150), extensive contralateral connectivity, novel indirect light inputs, and pathways onto descending neurons involved in feeding and reproductive behavior. Sparse monosynaptic output to higher-order and neurosecretory cells motivates integration of single-cell transcriptomes and receptor maps, which suggest additional neuropeptides and paracrine enrichment of the network. A limitations section lists undercounting risks and notes extra Princeton synapse predictions that increase some LNITP-mediated connections without changing conclusions.
summaries.advanced: The ~240 versus 150 comparison is the authors’ recensus including newly identified dorsal neurons, not an independent census in this extract. Connectivity is thresholded (>4 synapses) and omits gap junctions; photoreceptor proofreading was incomplete. Paracrine maps are putative. FlyWire and hemibrain are female; there is no male clock connectome here. Catalog metadata list the journal as bioRxiv, but the PDF and DOI are Nature Communications.

plain_language_summary: The fly’s daily clock was thought to be about 150 neurons. Using a whole-brain wiring map, this team finds more clock cells, left–right connections, extra light routes, and a likely big role for peptide signals rather than only direct synapses.

ocar.opportunity: Peripheral temperature cues must reach central circadian networks so animals can remodel sleep and wake, but the integration logic in Drosophila was unclear.
ocar.challenge: How circadian circuits combine thermosensory and clock signals to set sleep/wake patterns, especially the evening activity peak, remained unknown.
ocar.action: Yuan, Li, and Guo in PLoS Biology (2024) use the FlyWire EM connectome to place lateral posterior neurons (LPNs) as integration nodes, then combine connectomics with genetic manipulation, optogenetic calcium imaging, and behavioral assays.
ocar.resolution: LPNs receive both circadian and temperature-sensing input and promote sleep. Downstream of thermosensitive anterior cells they suppress activity-promoting LNds via allatostatin C; disrupting AstCR1 (RNAi in LNds or a mutant) impairs the heat-induced reduction of the evening activity peak. Cold-activated LNds stimulate LPNs via NPF–NPFR, forming negative feedback that limits the evening-peak increase in the cold.
ocar.future_work: Figure 7 models are mechanistic sketches integrating this paper with prior work; the extract does not quantify synapse counts on the highlighted edges. Temperature-sensory coverage in FlyWire is discussed as incomplete in the truncated closing of the extract.

summaries.beginner: Flies sleep and move differently when it is hot or cold. This study finds a small circadian cell group that hears both the clock and temperature sensors and uses peptide signals to keep evening activity in a safe range.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Biology (2024), Yuan, Li, and Guo use FlyWire to identify LPNs as nodes that integrate temperature into the circadian network. Connectome analysis plus genetics and behavior show an AC→LPN→LNd AstC pathway that promotes heat-induced evening sleep, and an LNd→LPN NPF–NPFR feedback that restrains cold-induced evening locomotion. Disrupting LPN–LNd communication via AstCR1 RNAi or mutation significantly impairs the heat-induced drop in the evening activity peak. The discussion frames the loop as seasonal energy management at dusk.
summaries.advanced: Causal claims rest on genetic and imaging experiments plus connectome anatomy; the extract does not report numeric synapse thresholds for the highlighted connections. “Novel peptidergic circadian feedback circuit” is the authors’ framing. DN1a and TPNs appear in the Fig. 7 model as additional temperature routes. FlyWire is a female brain reconstruction; sex differences are not addressed here.

plain_language_summary: Flies sleep and move differently when it is hot or cold. This study finds a small circadian cell group that hears both the clock and temperature sensors and uses peptide signals to keep evening activity in a safe range.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics image stacks now reach terabyte to petabyte scale with diverse appearance across regions and samples, so synapse detectors trained on tiny labeled fractions need to generalize out of domain.
ocar.challenge: Manual synapse annotation is slow, leaving training sets often smaller than 0.001% of test data, and domain-adaptation methods developed for natural images have lacked out-of-domain connectomics benchmarks.
ocar.action: Wu, Li, Gupta, Shinomiya, Gunn, Polilov, Pfister, Chklovskii, and Wei present an ISBI 2023 challenge paper (arXiv:2302.00545) that annotates 14 image chunks from biologically diverse Megaphragma viggianii brain regions in three whole-brain datasets.
ocar.resolution: The paper defines a synapse-detection challenge (pre- and postsynaptic points in 3D EM) aimed at pushing out-of-domain generalization methods for large-scale connectomics, analogous in spirit to CREMI but focused on domain shift in a miniature wasp.
ocar.future_work: The selected extract is a challenge announcement plus author biographies; winning algorithms, leaderboards, and quantitative detector scores are not in this text.

summaries.beginner: Computers that find synapses are usually trained on a tiny labeled patch and then asked to work on a huge, differently looking brain. This paper sets up a contest on microwasp volumes so methods can be tested when the training and test images do not match.
summaries.intermediate: On arXiv (2302.00545, February 2023), framed as an ISBI 2023 challenge, Wu and colleagues motivate out-of-domain synapse detection for terabyte-to-petabyte EM. They annotate 14 chunks from diverse brain regions of Megaphragma viggianii across three whole-brain datasets, with presynapses and postsynapses as 3D points. The stated goal is to evaluate domain-adaptation and generalization methods that have been less tested on connectomics for lack of benchmarks. CREMI is cited as a prior in-domain circuit-reconstruction challenge.
summaries.advanced: This is a challenge description, not a completed method comparison. No algorithm performance numbers appear in the selected extract. The 0.001% training-versus-test figure is the authors’ characterization of typical label scarcity. Organism in the catalog is empty; the PDF specifies the miniature wasp Megaphragma viggianii.

plain_language_summary: Computers that find synapses are usually trained on a tiny labeled patch and then asked to work on a huge, differently looking brain. This paper sets up a contest on microwasp volumes so methods can be tested when the training and test images do not match.

ocar.opportunity: Defense and commercial edge learning still needs more efficient, robust, generalizable networks, and large neuroimaging plus synapse-resolution connectomes could supply architectural constraints.
ocar.challenge: Deep networks remain data-inefficient, power-hungry, and weak at generalization, while translating biological structure into machine-learning gains is not automatic.
ocar.action: Johnson, Robinson, Vallabha, Joyce, Matelsky and colleagues (arXiv:2305.17300, May 2023; catalog venue Defense + Commercial Sensing / SPIE) describe a pipeline: motif discovery for neural architecture search, analysis of the fly heading-direction circuit, fly memory circuitry for generative replay, and mammalian-cortex constraints on transformers.
ocar.resolution: A novel heading-circuit connectivity pattern was implemented and demonstrated as sensor fusion on a robot. Generative replay inspired by fly memory circuitry improved accuracy by over 20% in an incremental class-learning scenario. Cortex-inspired constraints increased robustness on the most challenging CIFAR-10-C examples while reducing learnable attention parameters by over an order of magnitude.
ocar.future_work: The authors call for sustained BRAIN Initiative-scale datasets, neuromorphic implementations, and studies of learning rules in highly recurrent heterogeneous networks. Transformer work is described as begun; transfer to audio, video, and RF on existing neuromorphic platforms is proposed rather than demonstrated here.

summaries.beginner: Brain wiring diagrams might teach computers to learn with less data and power. This group tries several fly- and cortex-inspired tricks—repeated motifs, a heading circuit on a robot, memory replay, and trimmed attention—and reports gains on a few test tasks.
summaries.intermediate: This extract is the May 2023 arXiv preprint of a SPIE Defense + Commercial Sensing paper by Johnson and colleagues at JHU/APL. They outline four uses of large neuroimaging/connectome data: motif-based architecture search, a fly heading-direction circuit for visual–angular-velocity fusion on a robot, a generative-replay method from fly memory circuitry (>20% accuracy gain in incremental class learning), and cortex-inspired constraints on transformers (better robustness on the hardest CIFAR-10-C examples, attention parameters cut by more than 10×). Acknowledgments credit FlyEM and MICrONS datasets and BossDB storage.
summaries.advanced: Title and authors match the catalog SPIE entry; the PDF is the arXiv preprint (different DOI). The four results are separate case studies, not one unified benchmark. “Over 20%” and “over an order of magnitude” are author-reported; base models and exact splits are not in the selected text. Mammalian-cortex transformer work is preliminary. Robotics and CIFAR results should not be read as connectomic reconstruction methods.

plain_language_summary: Brain wiring diagrams might teach computers to learn with less data and power. This group tries several fly- and cortex-inspired tricks—repeated motifs, a heading circuit on a robot, memory replay, and trimmed attention—and reports gains on a few test tasks.

ocar.opportunity: Super-resolution optical microscopy visualizes molecules and sparse cells but not dense tissue context, while EM is comprehensive yet hard to pair with molecular labels in chemically fixed samples.
ocar.challenge: Dense mapping of brain architecture from millimeter regional to nanometer synaptic scales in diverse fixed preparations, including human diagnostic tissue, was lacking.
ocar.action: Michalska, Lyudchik, Velicky, Štefaničková, Watson and colleagues in Nature Biotechnology (2023) introduce Comprehensive Analysis of Tissues across Scales (CATS): fixation-compatible extracellular labeling plus STED or expansion microscopy to delineate cell surfaces and putative synaptic cleft regions.
ocar.resolution: CATS enabled 3D reconstruction of single synapses and mapping of connectivity via putative clefts. In mouse hippocampal mossy-fiber circuitry they reconstructed and quantified synaptic input and output of identified neurons, and they demonstrate labeling in human surgical and formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded diagnostic specimens. A deep-learning approach recalled about 82% of immunolabeled synapses at IoU threshold 0.2; putative-cleft inference used manual proofreading.
ocar.future_work: Throughput of 3D reconstruction was limited by manual cell-shape segmentation. Generalization to arbitrary synapse types needs a more diverse training set. Permeabilization labels only a few tens of micrometers from the surface, matched to 3D STED depth; expansion microscopy trades some structural fidelity for speed on conventional microscopes.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes see every cell but not easily every molecule; ordinary light microscopes see molecules but not the dense packing of tissue. This method stains the spaces between cells so light microscopy can map tissue and likely synapses from mouse hippocampus to human pathology samples.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Biotechnology (2023), Michalska, Danzl and colleagues present CATS, using extracellular labeling compatible with living (coCATS) or fixed (rCATS) tissue, then STED or expansion microscopy. They reconstruct mossy-fiber synaptic structure in mouse hippocampus and show applicability to rodent and human preparations including FFPE diagnostics. Putative synaptic cleft regions (pSCRs) support connectivity mapping after proofreading; a deep-learning detector recalled ~82% of immunolabeled synapses (IoU 0.2). Discussion contrasts unbiased extracellular contrast with sparse intracellular labels and notes organoid and native-brain applicability.
summaries.advanced: pSCRs are putative clefts, not EM-verified synaptic identities; the authors applied manual proofreading when inferring connections. The 82% recall is versus immunolabeling at a stated IoU, not a full connectome accuracy. Training data were dominated by excitatory mossy-fiber synapses. CATS is optical dense mapping, not a replacement for volume EM. Depth is limited by permeabilization and STED penetration unless expansion strategies are used.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes see every cell but not easily every molecule; ordinary light microscopes see molecules but not the dense packing of tissue. This method stains the spaces between cells so light microscopy can map tissue and likely synapses from mouse hippocampus to human pathology samples.

ocar.opportunity: The insect central complex is a conserved navigator, yet insects occupy diverse anatomical and ecological niches that must feed into that structure.
ocar.challenge: How a relatively invariant CX can incorporate species-specific sensory and state information is not obvious from adult anatomy alone.
ocar.action: Kandimalla, Omoto, Hong, and Hartenstein review in Journal of Comparative Physiology A (2023) the developmental lineages and tracts of CX input channels, overlaying that information on the Drosophila hemibrain connectome and on anatomical and physiological recordings in other insects.
ocar.resolution: They report neuropil- and lineage-specific innervation, connectivity, and activity profiles in CX input channels. They argue that neuroblast proliferative potential and lineage-based information channels allow modification of existing, novel, or deprecated modalities in a species-specific way, providing a substrate for diversification of navigational circuits. Extract enumerations include major fan-shaped-body large-field lineages such as DALcl2v and CP2d.
ocar.future_work: This is a review and synthesis, not a new connectome. Evolutionary hypotheses about lineage as an evolvable channel are posited. Hemibrain neuron counts in the extract are dataset enumerations, not independent biological replicates.

summaries.beginner: Insect brains grow from about a hundred stem cells per side, each producing a family of sister neurons with a shared path into the brain. This review argues those families are how different species plug new senses into a shared navigation center.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Comparative Physiology A (2023), Kandimalla and colleagues review input channels to the insect central complex through development and evolution. Insect hemispheres arise from ~100 neuroblasts whose lineages follow characteristic tracts; overlaying those tracts on the Drosophila hemibrain, plus comparative anatomy and physiology, shows lineage- and neuropil-specific innervation and activity. The fan-shaped body is treated as the most numerically complex CX compartment, with large-field inputs from a handful of major lineages (including DALcl2v and CP2d, with hemibrain counts given in the extract). The authors posit lineage architecture as the substrate for species-specific navigational circuit evolution.
summaries.advanced: Review article: no new EM volume. Hemibrain counts (for example DALcl2v right-hemisphere = 45 in one subpopulation description) are taken from the dataset as cited, not re-proofread here. Comparative claims mix Drosophila connectomics with recordings in other species. The evolutionary mechanism is a hypothesis. Catalog year/journal match the PDF (J Comp Physiol A 2023).

plain_language_summary: Insect brains grow from about a hundred stem cells per side, each producing a family of sister neurons with a shared path into the brain. This review argues those families are how different species plug new senses into a shared navigation center.

ocar.opportunity: Animals assign valence to stimuli from experience, but how mushroom-body memories are turned into specific actions such as running upwind is poorly understood.
ocar.challenge: Multiple mushroom-body compartments assign valence in parallel, yet they induce different amounts of upwind locomotion, so a downstream decoder was missing.
ocar.action: Aso, Yamada, Bushey, Hibbard, Sammons, Otsuna, Shuai, and Hige in eLife (2023) combine a photoactivation screen of new split-GAL4 drivers, EM connectomics, physiology, and behavior to identify UpWind Neurons (UpWiNs) postsynaptic to mushroom-body output neurons.
ocar.resolution: UpWiNs integrate inhibitory input from appetitive-memory MBONs and excitatory input from aversive-memory MBONs. After appetitive learning they respond more to reward-predicting odors as the inhibitory MBON depresses. Blocking UpWiNs impaired appetitive memory and reduced upwind locomotion during retrieval; photoactivation also increased the chance of returning to the site where activation ended.
ocar.future_work: Turning direction and walking speed still depend on the fly’s orientation to wind, so UpWiNs mark a transition from abstract valence to action rather than a complete motor program. Generality of the divergent-then-convergent architecture to vertebrates is analogical.

summaries.beginner: Flies that learned an odor predicts sugar will walk into the wind to find it. This paper finds a small group of neurons that read mushroom-body memory outputs and help turn that good-versus-bad signal into upwind walking.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2023), Aso and colleagues show that appetitive memories stored in different mushroom-body compartments drive different amounts of upwind locomotion. A split-GAL4 photoactivation screen plus EM connectomics identified UpWiNs postsynaptic to MBONs; they mix inhibition from appetitive compartments with excitation from aversive ones. Learning enhances UpWiN odor responses as the inhibitory MBON depresses. TNT or shibire manipulations impaired memory and upwind retrieval, and CsChrimson activation increased return probability to the termination site even without airflow in related assays. The editor’s evaluation calls the evidence convincing and of broad interest for how plasticity becomes action.
summaries.advanced: UpWiN identity is tied to specific split-GAL4 lines (SS33917 appears in Fig. 7). Memory and locomotion effects are loss- and gain-of-function in those drivers, not a full ablation of all anatomically similar cells. EM connectivity is used to place UpWiNs in the MBON graph; the extract does not quote synapse counts. Catalog datasets field is empty; the work uses EM connectomics of the fly brain without naming a public volume in the selected text.

plain_language_summary: Flies that learned an odor predicts sugar will walk into the wind to find it. This paper finds a small group of neurons that read mushroom-body memory outputs and help turn that good-versus-bad signal into upwind walking.

ocar.opportunity: Many animals navigate toward unseen goals using spatial maps organized as attractor networks, anchored to landmarks and reciprocally tied to motor control.
ocar.challenge: Drosophila connectomes reveal anatomical potential synapses, but navigation appears to depend on ongoing plasticity that continually reselects which of those synapses are functional.
ocar.action: Wilson reviews this progress in Annual Review of Neuroscience (2023), focusing on arthropod studies and the interaction of Hebbian rules, sensory feedback, attractor dynamics, and neuromodulation.
ocar.resolution: She argues that working memory as persistent activity and long-term memory as weights operate together: attractors store key variables while functional connectivity is constantly remodeled, explaining rapid map updates and how goals can be initialized as stable fixed points.
ocar.future_work: Strong in-vivo evidence for plasticity is cited mainly at ER→EPG synapses. Other proposed sites—protocerebral-bridge body-size calibration, velocity-to-head-direction weights, PFL3 goal switching, and path integration downstream of hΔB neurons—remain hypotheses because synaptic weights are not observed directly. Connectome-constrained models with Hebbian rules are suggested as a testbed.

summaries.beginner: Animals can walk toward a place they cannot see because the brain keeps a map with a bump of activity that stands for direction or goal. This review says those maps are not a fixed wiring diagram: synapses are constantly chosen from a larger anatomical menu.
summaries.intermediate: In Annual Review of Neuroscience (2023), Wilson synthesizes arthropod navigation networks—attractors, landmark anchoring, and reciprocal motor links—with emphasis on the Drosophila connectome plus plasticity. Keywords include memory, menotaxis, path integration, head direction, dopamine, and coordinate transformation. The outlook rejects a clean split between activity-based working memory and weight-based long-term memory, arguing both run continuously under neuromodulatory control. She notes strong evidence at ER→EPG synapses (Fisher, Kim) and lists other candidate plastic sites from the literature.
summaries.advanced: This is a review. Plasticity at sites other than ER→EPG is explicitly “suggested” or “proposed” in cited work, not established here. The Drosophila connectome supplies anatomical potential synapses; functional selection is inferred. Catalog organism is fly, matching the review’s focus, though the opening frames navigation more broadly across animals.

plain_language_summary: Animals can walk toward a place they cannot see because the brain keeps a map with a bump of activity that stands for direction or goal. This review says those maps are not a fixed wiring diagram: synapses are constantly chosen from a larger anatomical menu.

ocar.opportunity: Neuromodulation often assumes a cell class uniformly expresses a receptor so its computation can be retuned as a whole; heterogeneous receptor expression could instead retune subclasses for different odor scenes.
ocar.challenge: Consequences of heterogeneous rather than uniform serotonin (5-HT) receptor co-expression within Drosophila olfactory projection neurons were unexplored.
ocar.action: Jonaitis, Mazri, Sizemore, Ralston, Salman, Fletcher, Matheny, Ramachandra, and Dacks post on bioRxiv (2023) maps of 5-HT receptor co-expression in two PN populations, their glomerular innervation, downstream connectomic overlap, and odor-evoked modulation.
ocar.resolution: Two PN populations co-express 5-HT receptors heterogeneously, innervate different glomerular combinations, show little convergence onto shared downstream partners, and are differentially modulated by 5-HT according to receptor profile and odor tuning.
ocar.future_work: The discussion notes that receptor diversity may mark already-known morphological subdivisions (uniglomerular, multiglomerular, panglomerular v-PNs) rather than an independent axis. Causal necessity of each receptor combination is not established in the selected extract, which runs into the reference list.

summaries.beginner: Serotonin is often treated as a volume knob for a whole cell class. In the fly nose’s output cells, different neurons carry different serotonin receptor mixes, so the same chemical can retune different odors differently.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (21 June 2023), Jonaitis, Mazri, Dacks and colleagues contrast uniform versus heterogeneous 5-HT receptor expression in Drosophila olfactory projection neurons. They report that two PN populations co-express all 5-HT receptors non-uniformly, that receptor-defined subsets innervate different glomeruli, that connectomics shows little downstream convergence among those subsets, and that 5-HT differentially modulates their odor-evoked responses. The implication is stimulus-specific neuromodulation inside a nominal cell class, depending on the odor scene each neuron reports.
summaries.advanced: The extract’s discussion is truncated into references; quantitative physiology (which odors, effect sizes) is not in the selected text. Connectomic “little convergence” is stated without synapse counts here. Receptor co-expression may collinear with known v-PN morphological classes. This is a preprint. Catalog dimension is neuroanatomy; the paper is equally physiology plus connectomics of the antennal lobe.

plain_language_summary: Serotonin is often treated as a volume knob for a whole cell class. In the fly nose’s output cells, different neurons carry different serotonin receptor mixes, so the same chemical can retune different odors differently.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans has EM connectomes for both sexes and several stages, but sample sizes are tiny; fluorescent synaptic reporters could scale analysis of synapse number, size, intensity, and position.
ocar.challenge: Heterogeneous neurite morphology, fluorescence, and imaging parameters make unbiased high-throughput quantification of punctate synaptic signals difficult.
ocar.action: Majeed, Han, Zhang, Cao, Liao, Hobert, and Lu post on bioRxiv (2023) WormPsyQi, an automated image-analysis pipeline, plus 30 transgenic strains labeling chemical synapses (CLA-1, RAB-3, GRASP) or electrical synapses (innexin reporters).
ocar.resolution: WormPsyQi quantified synaptic features across nervous-system regions, developmental stages, and sexes despite substantial imaging heterogeneity, and the authors note the same pipeline can apply to other punctate signals such as receptors or cell-adhesion molecules.
ocar.future_work: Reporters are proxies: GRASP visualizes NLG-1 proximity, not every chemical synapse. Multicopy arrays can mislocalize; lines from the same injection vary. Dim cytoplasmic markers yield discontinuous neurite masks and undercounting. Endogenous tags and single-copy transgenes are recommended to approach ground truth versus EM.

summaries.beginner: Seeing every synapse in the worm with electron microscopy is slow. This team shares fluorescent worm strains and software that count synapse-like dots in many animals, stages, and both sexes.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (1 November 2023) as a Life Resource, Majeed, Han, Zhang, Hobert, Lu and colleagues describe WormPsyQi and 30 strains labeling chemical or electrical synapses throughout the C. elegans nervous system. The pipeline is meant to reduce human bias while quantifying number, size, intensity, and spatial distribution of puncta. Introduction places the resource against existing EM connectomes (White, Cook, Witvliet, dauer maps) whose sample sizes remain small. Limitations discuss GRASP as an NLG-1 proxy, overexpression artifacts, and mask failures when cytoplasmic signal is dim.
summaries.advanced: This is not a new EM connectome. Puncta are fluorescent proxies; the authors themselves warn of discrepancies with EM reconstructions in figures not fully captured here. “High-throughput” is relative to manual puncta scoring, not to whole-animal EM. Catalog method lists electron microscopy because of that comparison, but the toolkit is light-microscopy plus analysis.

plain_language_summary: Seeing every synapse in the worm with electron microscopy is slow. This team shares fluorescent worm strains and software that count synapse-like dots in many animals, stages, and both sexes.

ocar.opportunity: Whether a synapse is excitatory or inhibitory is essential for circuit models, yet polarity remains sparse even in C. elegans, where simulations such as OpenWorm would benefit from more complete signs.
ocar.challenge: High-throughput synapse finding outpaces low-throughput polarity assays, so computational inference from limited genetic and network information is needed.
ocar.action: Harris, Wytock, and Kovács in Advanced Science (2022) infer polarity in three data regimes: a connectome model (CM) using neurotransmitter and receptor expression plus wiring rules; a spatial CM trained with known polarities but without wiring rules; and a generalized CM as a network sign-prediction problem when expression and rules are unavailable.
ocar.resolution: The CM resolves 356 synaptic polarities in addition to 1,752 known ones. The spatial CM infers the polarity of 81% of the CM-resolved connections at greater than 95% precision and infers 147 of the remaining unknown polarities.
ocar.future_work: Results are computational inferences, not new electrophysiology. The selected extract’s discussion is largely references and a Zenodo data DOI; assumptions beyond the abstract are not fully captured. Signs remain to be integrated into dynamical simulators as the authors motivate.

summaries.beginner: Knowing who connects to whom is not enough: you also need plus versus minus. This paper guesses excitatory versus inhibitory synapses in the worm from genes, receptors, and network patterns, filling in hundreds of missing signs on the computer.
summaries.intermediate: In Advanced Science (2022), Harris, Wytock, and Kovács treat synaptic polarity inference on the C. elegans connectome under three information settings. With neurotransmitter/receptor expression and a wiring-rule network, the connectome model adds 356 polarities to 1,752 already known. Adding known polarities as training data, the spatial connectome model recovers 81% of those CM-resolved signs at >95% precision and proposes 147 further unknowns. Without expression or rules, polarity is cast as signed-network prediction, illustrated with a generalized CM. Data are deposited at Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.6342306).
summaries.advanced: Polarities are inferred, not measured. The 81% / >95% figures are for recovery of CM-resolved connections, not of an independent electrophysiological gold standard. Catalog journal string is “Advancement of science”; the PDF is Advanced Science. Human connectome scale is motivational in the introduction, not an evaluation setting.

plain_language_summary: Knowing who connects to whom is not enough: you also need plus versus minus. This paper guesses excitatory versus inhibitory synapses in the worm from genes, receptors, and network patterns, filling in hundreds of missing signs on the computer.

ocar.opportunity: Petascale EM and X-ray microtomography datasets could seed reusable submicron atlases if annotations and neuroanatomical metadata were comparable across labs.
ocar.challenge: Image interfaces have been standardized more than annotations: heterogeneous formats force specialists to parse raw labels, blocking secondary analysis.
ocar.action: Sanchez, Moore, Johnson, Wester, Lichtman, and Gray-Roncal in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2022) outline design considerations for connectomics annotation metadata and a usecase on a recent large-scale dataset (H01), later extended to Kasthuri et al. 2015.
ocar.resolution: They describe a proof-of-concept query portal over tabular/RAMON-like metadata stored in MongoDB, arguing that community-adopted standards plus simple query tools would amplify investment in reconstruction.
ocar.future_work: The authors call the implementation demonstration-quality: only MongoDB was tried, the UI had limited design cycles, and translating diverse storage formats into a common schema is left as future work. They hope for a centralized multi-dataset portal once standards exist.

summaries.beginner: Huge electron-microscope brains are hard to reuse because every lab stores cell and synapse labels differently. This perspective argues for shared metadata so anyone can query “what is this object?” without downloading raw annotation dumps.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (May 2022), Sanchez, Moore, Gray-Roncal and colleagues argue that EM and XRM connectomics need standardized annotation metadata, not only standardized image APIs. They share design considerations and a usecase built for a large-scale dataset, with a later query page for Kasthuri et al. (2015) in addition to H01. The software is a proof of concept for queryability and reproducibility. Keywords listed are connectome, annotation, software, standard, queries, reproducibility.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective/proof of concept, not a new reconstruction. Database and UI choices were not systematically benchmarked. “Recent large-scale dataset” in the abstract is H01 in the body. Catalog dimension is proofreading because annotations are the object, but the contribution is infrastructure/metadata rather than a proofreading algorithm.

plain_language_summary: Huge electron-microscope brains are hard to reuse because every lab stores cell and synapse labels differently. This perspective argues for shared metadata so anyone can query “what is this object?” without downloading raw annotation dumps.

ocar.opportunity: Connection strengths in neuronal networks are heavy-tailed across species, with a few pairs far stronger than most, suggesting a shared generative mechanism.
ocar.challenge: It was unclear whether those tails require species-specific biophysics or can emerge from simple self-organization, and how clustering would arise in the same framework.
ocar.action: Lynn, Holmes, and Palmer (bioRxiv 31 May 2022; catalog DOI is the later Nature Physics paper) propose a minimal model: synapses are pruned at random while remaining strength rearranges under a mixture of Hebbian and random growth, then extend it with activity correlations.
ocar.resolution: Networks become scale-free with exponent γ = 1 + 1/p that depends only on the probability p of Hebbian versus random growth. Activity-dependent plasticity additionally produces clustering. Predictions are compared to EM connectomes including the Drosophila central brain (14 million synapses among more than 21 thousand neurons; 99% of pairs unconnected; 50% of connected pairs linked by a single synapse), optic medulla, C. elegans, Platynereis, and mouse retina.
ocar.future_work: Clustering comparisons use symmetrized connectomes. The authors propose spike-timing-dependent plasticity and more realistic activity models to generate the directed asymmetries of real connectomes. The model is intentionally minimal, not a biophysical synapse simulator.

summaries.beginner: In many animals a few neuron pairs are wired much more strongly than everyone else. This paper shows a simple grow-and-prune rule, mixing “fire together, wire together” with randomness, that can grow those heavy tails and also clumps of connections.
summaries.intermediate: The PDF is the May 2022 bioRxiv preprint of work later indexed under Nature Physics DOI 10.1038/s41567-023-02332-9. Lynn, Holmes, and Palmer fit heavy-tailed strengths across several EM connectomes and introduce a model whose power-law exponent depends only on the Hebbian-growth probability. Adding correlated activity yields clustering, another widespread connectome feature. Drosophila hemibrain-scale statistics in the extract include 14 million synapses, >21k neurons, 99% unconnected pairs, and 50% of connected pairs with one synapse. Methods list directed versus symmetrized versions for different figure comparisons.
summaries.advanced: Catalog journal is bioRxiv while the uuid is the Nature Physics DOI; title and authors match. γ = 1 + 1/p is a model derivation, not a measured exponent for every species in the extract. “Several animals” / four-species framing in the catalog abstract is specified in the PDF methods as fly (two regions), worm, Platynereis, and mouse retina. Clustering tests use symmetrized graphs.

plain_language_summary: In many animals a few neuron pairs are wired much more strongly than everyone else. This paper shows a simple grow-and-prune rule, mixing “fire together, wire together” with randomness, that can grow those heavy tails and also clumps of connections.

ocar.opportunity: Multisensory integration is essential for reducing uncertainty and guiding behavior, but molecular, synaptic, and circuit mechanisms remain poorly understood; C. elegans offers a complete connectome, genetics, and sensitive sensors.
ocar.challenge: MSI was studied mainly in mammals, while worm paradigms of convergence at sensory versus interneuron levels needed a comparative synthesis.
ocar.action: Yu, Xue, and Chen review in Brain Sciences (2022) representative C. elegans MSI cases, summarize mechanisms, and compare them with mammalian systems.
ocar.resolution: They argue that despite phylogenetic distance, the worm provides unique insight into flexible, adaptive multisensory behavior, especially because whole-nervous-system imaging at single-neuron resolution during behavior is uniquely feasible.
ocar.future_work: This is a narrative review with no new experiments. The authors anticipate combining brain-wide recordings with theory and new optical/synthetic tools. They note that current microscopy still cannot capture all neurons of a mammalian functional network.

summaries.beginner: Animals mix sight, smell, touch, and more into one decision. This review collects how the tiny worm does that mixing and argues we can watch almost every neuron at once, something we cannot yet do in mammals.
summaries.intermediate: In Brain Sciences (2022), Yu, Xue, and Chen review multisensory integration in C. elegans versus mammals. They emphasize convergence at sensory-neuron or interneuron levels, the worm’s mapped connectome and genetic tools, and the promise of whole-brain imaging during behavior. Conclusions contrast mammalian cortical MSI literature with worm circuit-level cases and fund the perspective via a China STI2030 brain-science grant. Keywords include sensory processing, modality, and neural plasticity.
summaries.advanced: Narrative review: no original circuit reconstruction or new MSI experiment. Comparative claims are qualitative. “Completely mapped neural connectome” refers to the classical C. elegans wiring plus later updates cited in the field, not a new map here. Catalog journal string is “Brain Science”; the PDF is Brain Sci. 2022, 12, 1368.

plain_language_summary: Animals mix sight, smell, touch, and more into one decision. This review collects how the tiny worm does that mixing and argues we can watch almost every neuron at once, something we cannot yet do in mammals.

ocar.opportunity: How the detailed topology of a neural circuit shapes behavior is a central question; the C. elegans nociceptive circuit uses the same neurons in both sexes but wires them differently.
ocar.challenge: Nociceptive sensory neurons respond similarly in the two sexes, yet aversive behaviors are sexually dimorphic, so downstream network topology may be causal rather than sensory encoding.
ocar.action: Pechuk, Goldman, Salzberg, Chaubey, Bola, Hoffman, Enderson, Miller, Reger, Portman, Ferkey, Schneidman, and Oren-Suissa (Current Biology 2022; catalog DOI 10.2139/ssrn.4030988) learn and simulate network models that replicate the dimorphic behaviors and predict simple rewirings that would switch sex-typical responses.
ocar.resolution: Experimental synaptic rewirings flipped behavior between the sexes. When presented with aversive cues, rewired males were compromised in finding mating partners, suggesting that topologies enabling efficient avoidance carry a reproductive cost.
ocar.future_work: The catalog abstract does not specify which synapses were rewired or the model class beyond network simulations; those details would require the correct full text.

summaries.beginner: Male and female worms can sense a nasty cue with the same sensory cells but then act differently. This paper models the downstream wiring, tweaks a few connections, and reports that behavior—and even mating success—can flip with those tweaks.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2022; SSRN/catalog DOI 10.2139/ssrn.4030988), Pechuk, Oren-Suissa, Schneidman and colleagues study sexually dimorphic nociception in C. elegans. Sensory responses are similar across sexes while behavior is not. Network models fitted to the dimorphic behaviors predicted minimal rewirings that experimentally switched sex-typical avoidance. Rewired males were worse at finding mates in the presence of aversive cues, which the authors interpret as a reproductive cost of efficient nociceptive topologies.
summaries.advanced: PDF extract mismatch: the selected text is Richter and Schneidman, PNAS 2025, “Building the connectome of a small brain with a simple stochastic developmental generative model,” not Pechuk et al. on nociceptive-circuit rewiring. OCAR and summaries use the catalog abstract only; no numbers, synapse identities, or model details were taken from the mismatched PDF. Catalog venue is Current Biology.

plain_language_summary: Male and female worms can sense a nasty cue with the same sensory cells but then act differently. This paper models the downstream wiring, tweaks a few connections, and reports that behavior—and even mating success—can flip with those tweaks.

ocar.opportunity: Dense EM reconstruction is extremely laborious; sparse neuron tracing from seed masks could recover specific morphologies with less manual work.
ocar.challenge: Sparse reconstruction on highly anisotropic EM volumes is understudied, interlayer context is weak, and misalignment breaks traces in large-scale data.
ocar.action: Liu, Hong, Chen, Xie, Tang, and Han in Biomedical Signal Processing and Control (2021) combine convolutional LSTMs for inter-slice spatial context, a lightweight U-Net for intra-slice cues, recursive training, and a shift-estimation and correction module.
ocar.resolution: They report better performance than other methods on two highly anisotropic datasets, claim a first application of a recurrent network to neuron tracing, and state that shift correction increased traced neuron length.
ocar.future_work: The selected extract does not name the two datasets or quote numeric scores. Dense voxel morphology is not the goal; the system traces from seeds. Recursive training and alignment correction remain engineering choices whose failure modes are not fully described in the truncated PDF text.

summaries.beginner: Following one neuron through a stack of stretched electron-microscope slices is hard when the slices do not line up. This system uses a memory network plus a U-Net, starting from a seed, to keep tracing despite those jumps.
summaries.intermediate: In Biomedical Signal Processing and Control (2021), Liu, Han and colleagues present an AI system for sparse neuron tracing on anisotropic EM. ConvLSTMs estimate context between adjacent sections, a lightweight U-Net supplies in-plane information, recursive training is used to boost performance, and a shift-estimation module targets misalignment. They position sparse tracing as a less-studied alternative to dense segmentation and claim SOTA on two highly anisotropic datasets plus a first RNN use for this task. The introduction contrasts thousands of human hours for some dense reconstructions with the needs of type-specific sparse work.
summaries.advanced: No numeric metrics or dataset names appear in the selected extract, so those SOTA claims cannot be checked here. “First RNN for neuron tracing” is an authorship claim. Catalog stages include alignment and proofreading; the method is tracing with an alignment-correction module, not a general aligner or proofreading UI. Competing-interest and funding statements are present; scientific caveats beyond truncation are limited.

plain_language_summary: Following one neuron through a stack of stretched electron-microscope slices is hard when the slices do not line up. This system uses a memory network plus a U-Net, starting from a seed, to keep tracing despite those jumps.

ocar.opportunity: Gustatory receptor neurons report caloric versus harmful compounds and thereby bound what the brain can use for feeding decisions; their synaptic transmit-and-receive pattern in the adult fly brain was unmapped.
ocar.challenge: Whether labellar axons are organized by taste modality and whether they synapse on one another—as other sensory axons do—was unknown at EM resolution.
ocar.action: Engert, Sterne, Bock, and Scott in eLife (2022) reconstructed 87 gustatory projections from the proboscis labellum in the right hemisphere and 57 in the left of a whole-brain EM volume, clustering them by morphology and connectivity.
ocar.resolution: GRNs have nearly equal interspersed pre- and postsynaptic sites and extensive axon–axon connectivity. Clustering yielded six groups likely corresponding to taste modalities, with the vast majority of synapses within groups. About 39% of GRN input comes from other GRNs, paralleling ORN–ORN connectivity in olfaction.
ocar.future_work: Modality assignments (bitter, candidate low-salt Ir94e, high salt, sugar, water) are anatomical correlations with light-level maps and remain tentative until second-order neurons are identified and physiologically tested. Left and right counts differ; not all labellar axons were reconstructed.

summaries.beginner: Taste cells from the fly’s mouthparts send axons into the brain that talk not only to other cells but also to each other. This reconstruction shows those axons cluster by taste type and mostly synapse within their own group.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2022), Engert, Sterne, Bock, and Scott reconstruct the majority of labellar gustatory axons in a whole adult Drosophila EM volume (87 right, 57 left). Morphology- and connectivity-based clustering gives six groups interpreted as taste modalities, with nearly equal pre- and postsynaptic sites along axons and most connections inside groups. Discussion compares ~39% GRN-from-GRN input to ~40% ORN-from-ORN input in adult olfactory glomeruli and to larval GRN interconnectivity. The editor’s evaluation highlights the match to published functional taste classes via light-level anatomy.
summaries.advanced: Catalog journal is listed as bioRxiv; the PDF and DOI are eLife. Six-group modality labels are anatomical, not new calcium imaging in this paper. Hemisphere imbalance (87 vs 57) means the map is not fully bilateral. “Majority of labellar gustatory axons” is the authors’ completeness claim. Functional roles of axon–axon synapses (signal enhancement versus dynamic range) are suggested, not measured here.

plain_language_summary: Taste cells from the fly’s mouthparts send axons into the brain that talk not only to other cells but also to each other. This reconstruction shows those axons cluster by taste type and mostly synapse within their own group.

ocar.opportunity: New EM reconstructions, live imaging, omics, and genetics have expanded how we can study both the wiring of circuits and their long-term maintenance.
ocar.challenge: Cellular and subcellular synaptic specificity must be established and then maintained for years while remaining plastic enough for learning, and the molecular rules are still incomplete.
ocar.action: Heckman and Doe review in Journal of Neuroscience (2021) mechanisms of synaptic specificity—chemoaffinity and cell-surface cues, secreted signals, neuron–glia interactions, and activity—and mechanisms of maintenance via ECM, adhesion molecules, scaffolds, and the cytoskeleton.
ocar.resolution: They synthesize how a rigid support network allows synapses to persist, while opposing processes in regions such as hippocampus permit structural modification. Connectomes supply maps of stereotyped and variable connections that ground these principles.
ocar.future_work: The review flags stochastic versus deterministic wiring as an open contrast and asks how establishment/maintenance principles could prevent or restore synapse loss in disease. Those applications are not demonstrated here.

summaries.beginner: Brains must wire the right partners together and then keep those contacts for years without freezing all change. This review walks through the molecular and cellular rules that build and maintain circuits, using connectomes as maps.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neuroscience (February 2021), Heckman and Doe review circuit establishment and maintenance. They start from partner-derived cues for cellular synaptic specificity, revisit chemoaffinity from Langley and Sperry, and incorporate secreted cues, glia, and activity. Maintenance is attributed to ECM, CAMs, intracellular scaffolds, and cytoskeleton, with hippocampal dynamism as a counterexample. EM connectomes of model organisms are cited as providing stereotyped and variable connection maps that let these hypotheses be tested.
summaries.advanced: Review article with duplicated abstract text in the catalog metadata. No new reconstruction. Disease-therapy framing is prospective. The extract is truncated before a complete future-work close. Catalog method lists electron microscopy because connectomes are a data source, not because this paper presents a new EM volume.

plain_language_summary: Brains must wire the right partners together and then keep those contacts for years without freezing all change. This review walks through the molecular and cellular rules that build and maintain circuits, using connectomes as maps.

ocar.opportunity: Mammalian neuromuscular junctions reorganize after birth from poly-innervation toward Henneman’s size-principle recruitment; a complete wiring view across ages could reveal the ordering rule.
ocar.challenge: Neonatal motor units are large and overlapping, NMJs can be co-innervated by many axons, and some fibers have multiple endplates, so how non-overlapping adult motor units emerge was unclear.
ocar.action: Meirovitch, Kang, Draft, Pavarino, Henao Echeverri, Yang, Turney, Berger, Peleg, Montero-Crespo, Schalek, Lu, Livet, Tapia, and Lichtman post on bioRxiv (2021; this version 10 January 2023) serial-section SEM at birth plus Brainbow and XFP fluorescent reconstructions at later ages.
ocar.resolution: Axons prune about 85% of branches in the first two postnatal weeks, with an about 8-fold reduction in multi-axon NMJs and an about 6-fold reduction in fibers with more than one NMJ. Co-innervation persists longest among neurons nearby in an abstract rank order, likely reflecting activity similarity, and the same ranking governs both local NMJ competition and millimeter-scale contests. At birth no axon was the sole input to any fiber, and >30% of fibers had two or rarely three endplates in this neck muscle.
ocar.future_work: The activity-ranking link is inferred from fiber properties and NMJ distances, not simultaneous motor-unit recordings. Interscutularis is a neck muscle with many dual-endplate fibers; generality to other muscles is not proven in the extract. Ranking at birth is described as subtle because overlap is still high.

summaries.beginner: Baby muscles are wired in a messy many-to-many pattern that later becomes one axon per muscle fiber, recruited from small to large. This team maps that cleanup and finds axons stay partners longest with others that rank near them, probably because they fire similarly.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (this extract 10 January 2023), Meirovitch, Lichtman and colleagues reconstruct mouse neuromuscular connectomes at birth (ssSEM), one week, and adult (Brainbow/XFP). They report ~85% axonal branch pruning in two weeks, ~8-fold drop in poly-innervated NMJs, and ~6-fold drop in multi-endplate fibers. Simplification follows a global rank-order co-innervation rule rather than haphazard loss, which they relate to Henneman recruitment. Discussion adds that all motor-unit classes prune, size is already broadly distributed at birth, and co-innervation is graded by motor-unit size rather than a strict fiber-type binary.
summaries.advanced: Percentages in the abstract are the authors’ summary of their reconstructions; the extract does not restate raw axon counts. Rank order is an inferred embedding, not a measured firing-rate sequence. Dual endplates are common in this neck muscle historically; other muscles may differ. Catalog dimension is image-acquisition because of ssSEM, but the scientific payload is developmental graph analysis of connectivity.

plain_language_summary: Baby muscles are wired in a messy many-to-many pattern that later becomes one axon per muscle fiber, recruited from small to large. This team maps that cleanup and finds axons stay partners longest with others that rank near them, probably because they fire similarly.

ocar.opportunity: Platynereis dumerilii young worms are small enough for whole-body volume EM and single-cell sequencing, enabling a complete rope-ladder CNS tracing plus multimodal cellular atlases in a lophotrochozoan.
ocar.challenge: The community needed a current overview of natural history, methods, and recent connectomic advantages to expand the model beyond its classical evo-devo uses.
ocar.action: Özpolat, Randel, Williams, Bezares-Calderón, Jékely, Tessmar-Raible, Raible, Arendt and many co-authors review in EvoDevo (2021) habitat, life cycle, research history, and current topics including connectomics.
ocar.resolution: They highlight tracing of all neurons in the young worm’s rope-ladder CNS and construction of multimodal atlases as unique recent strengths, alongside genetics, regeneration, chronobiology, and ecology.
ocar.future_work: This is a community review, not a methods paper with reconstruction metrics or proofreading protocols. Connectomic details live in the cited primary volumes. The aim stated is to stimulate interest and grow the user community.

summaries.beginner: Platynereis is a marine worm used for development and evolution, and now also for mapping every neuron in a tiny whole body. This review introduces the animal and why its young stages suit volume electron microscopy.
summaries.intermediate: In EvoDevo (2021), Özpolat, Randel, Williams, Bezares-Calderón, Jékely, Tessmar-Raible, Raible, Arendt and colleagues review Platynereis dumerilii as a model. After habitat and pelago-benthic life cycle, they survey uses from regeneration and lunar clocks to, most recently, whole-body volume EM and single-cell genomics. The unique selling point for connectomics is the young worm’s size, enabling tracing of all neurons in a rope-ladder CNS and multimodal cellular atlases. The article is explicitly a community overview of topics and methodologies.
summaries.advanced: Review, not a new segmentation method despite the catalog dimension. No synapse counts or imaging resolutions are in the selected extract. “Tracing of all neurons” refers to cited young-worm reconstructions, not a dataset released in this paper. Organism tag “other” matches a non-fly/mouse/elegans model (annelid).

plain_language_summary: Platynereis is a marine worm used for development and evolution, and now also for mapping every neuron in a tiny whole body. This review introduces the animal and why its young stages suit volume electron microscopy.

ocar.opportunity: Voxel-wise CNN segmentation of terabyte-to-petabyte EM is costly and accumulates merge errors; a cheaper route to the connectivity graph would help labs under schedule and resource limits.
ocar.challenge: Conventional methods label every voxel, are not optimized for graph generation, and are sensitive to alignment and noise when scaled.
ocar.action: Drenkow, Joyce, Matelsky, Heiko, Larabi, Wester, Kleissas, Johnson, and Gray-Roncal post on bioRxiv (2020) a multi-agent path-finding approach: virtual agents with cheap potential-field sensors avoid membranes, find synapses, and share information while traversing 3D volumes.
ocar.resolution: The swarm produces a sparse segmentation of pathways plus connectivity, skeleton similarity, and path length. The authors report meeting or exceeding state-of-the-art performance at substantially lower computational cost, and note CPU parallelizability.
ocar.future_work: Agents miss some small processes and tortuous spine necks; processes that appear disconnected across slices remain hard. Dense morphology needs post-processing. More powerful sensing, learned policies, and transfer to other datasets are proposed. The method is also suggested for bronchial trees or road networks.

summaries.beginner: Instead of painting every pixel as a neuron, this method sends software “robots” through electron-microscope volumes to walk along cells and note synapses, aiming for a wiring graph at lower computer cost.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2 May 2020), Drenkow, Gray-Roncal and colleagues at JHU/APL recast EM neuron segmentation as autonomous navigation. Virtual agents follow local rules on potential fields to avoid membranes and locate synapses, yielding a sparse pathway map and a connectivity graph rather than a dense voxel labeling. They claim SOTA-competitive accuracy at much lower compute, with easy CPU parallelism. Funding includes IARPA MICrONS. Limitations include incomplete recovery of thin spines and sensitivity to slice discontinuities.
summaries.advanced: “Meet or exceed SOTA” is an authorship claim; the selected extract does not quote numeric table scores. Catalog lists Johnson among authors; the PDF includes Erik C. Johnson. This estimates a graph, not a proofread dense segmentation. MICrONS funding does not by itself mean the paper evaluates the public MICrONS volume; dataset identity is not named in the retained text.
